title: Study of Compounds: Ammonia
tagline: A gas that dissolves so readily it makes a fountain, and an alkali that behaves nothing like the hydroxides of metals.

overview.intro: Ammonia is the only common gas in this course that is alkaline, and almost every question about it comes back to that fact. It is made in the laboratory by warming an ammonium salt with a base, it dissolves in water far more readily than almost any other gas, and it reacts with acids to give the fertiliser salts that feed the world. The chapter follows the standard pattern — preparation, properties, reactions, uses — and adds the two demonstrations the examiner likes: the fountain experiment and the ammonia-soda test for the ammonium ion.

facts.label: Preparation
facts.value: Ammonium chloride heated with slaked lime in the laboratory.

facts.label: Molecule
facts.value: NH3, pyramidal, with one lone pair on nitrogen and a boiling point well below zero.

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: About 700 volumes of gas dissolve in one volume of water.

facts.label: Test
facts.value: Pungent smell and damp red litmus turning blue; white fumes with hydrogen chloride.

learningOutcomes: Describe the laboratory preparation of ammonia, including the drying agent and the collection method.
Explain the high solubility of ammonia in terms of hydrogen bonding and demonstrate it with a fountain.
Write equations for the reactions of ammonia with acids, with oxygen under a catalyst, and with metal salt solutions.
Describe the test for ammonia gas and the test for ammonium ions in a salt.
Give the principal uses of ammonia and connect each to a property discussed in the chapter.

blocks.text: The laboratory preparation heats a mixture of an ammonium salt and a base, because that is the simplest way to drive ammonia off from its salt. The usual pair is ammonium chloride with slaked lime, and the reaction is driven to completion by warming, since ammonia escapes as it forms. The gas is dried by passing it over quicklime — an alkali solid that will not react with an alkaline gas, unlike concentrated sulphuric acid or calcium chloride, both of which would either react with or absorb the ammonia. Collection is in an inverted jar by downward displacement of air, because ammonia is considerably lighter than air and would escape from a jar standing upright. Everything in the arrangement follows from two properties: it is basic, so the drying agent must be a base, and it is light, so the jar stands with its mouth downwards.

items: Reagents: ammonium chloride and slaked lime, both solids, mixed in a flask or test tube.
Drying: quicklime in a U-tube or drying bottle; never use concentrated sulphuric acid or calcium chloride.
Collection: in an inverted jar by downward displacement of air, since ammonia is lighter than air.
Delivery tube should be short and the apparatus set up promptly, because the gas escapes readily.

items.note: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2NH3 + 2H2O, with water forming as a second product.
Ammonia is less dense than air, so it collects at the closed top of the inverted jar and pushes air out below.

items.meaning: Calcium hydroxide, the base heated with ammonium chloride to release ammonia.
Calcium oxide, the drying agent chosen because it does not react with ammonia.
Collection of a gas lighter than air in an inverted jar, with the heavier air driven out below.

learn.title: Physical properties and why it dissolves so well

blocks.text: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a characteristically pungent smell that is easy to recognise once met, and it is markedly lighter than air. Its most dramatic property is solubility: at room temperature about seven hundred volumes of the gas dissolve in a single volume of water. The reason lies in the molecule itself. The nitrogen atom holds a lone pair and the three hydrogen atoms are bonded to a strongly electronegative atom, so molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding, and water molecules form even stronger attractions with them. The fountain experiment exploits this: when a trace of water meets the gas the pressure inside the flask collapses, and the atmosphere drives water up into the flask as a fine spray. The same solubility explains why a bottle of ammonia must be stoppered and why opening one releases a smell you notice across a room.

items: Colourless, pungent gas, distinctly less dense than air, so it collects in inverted jars.
About 700 volumes dissolve in one volume of water, giving a strongly alkaline solution.
Hydrogen bonding between molecules accounts for both its solubility and its easy liquefaction.
The aqueous solution turns red litmus blue, giving the standard test for the gas.

items.note: A drop of water drawn in dissolves the gas, the pressure falls sharply, and water surges up from the reservoir filling the jar.

items.text: A bottle left open in a lab
items.note: The smell spreads widely because so much dissolves in the moisture of the air and of your nasal passages.

items.meaning: Attraction between a hydrogen bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a nearby atom.
Demonstration in which rapid gas dissolution creates a pressure drop that draws liquid in as a spray.
Roughly seven hundred volumes of ammonia dissolve in one volume of water, the property both the fountain and the spray test rely on.

learn.title: Ammonia as a base: reactions with acids and salts

blocks.text: In water, ammonia accepts a proton from a water molecule to give ammonium ions and hydroxide ions, and that single equilibrium is why the solution behaves as a weak alkali: it turns litmus blue and neutralises acids, but it does not ionise completely the way sodium hydroxide does. With acids it gives ammonium salts directly, and these are the compounds used as fertilisers — ammonium chloride, ammonium sulphate and ammonium nitrate. With metal salt solutions the hydroxide ions precipitate metal hydroxides, and the pattern of colours is a practical identification tool: copper gives a light blue precipitate that dissolves in excess to a deep blue solution, iron(II) dirty green, iron(III) reddish brown, and zinc white and soluble in excess. That behaviour makes aqueous ammonia a second cation reagent alongside sodium hydroxide.

items: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-, which is the origin of all alkaline behaviour in aqueous ammonia.
With acids the reaction goes to completion: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl, dense white fumes of ammonium chloride.
Copper salt plus excess ammonia gives a deep blue tetrammine complex, the classic confirmatory test.
Zinc salts give a white precipitate that dissolves in excess, mirroring sodium hydroxide behaviour.

items.note: 2NH3 + H2SO4 → (NH4)2SO4, the ammonium sulphate used as a nitrogen fertiliser.
A pale precipitate forms first and then dissolves to a deep blue solution in excess ammonia.

learn.title: Oxidation of ammonia, sublimation and the ammonium test

blocks.text: Two further reactions complete the chemistry. Ammonia can be oxidised by oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at about 800 °C to give nitric oxide and water; this is the first step of the industrial route to nitric acid and shows ammonia acting as a reducing agent rather than a base. Heating ammonium chloride gives a white solid that reappears higher in the tube — not true sublimation but dissociation into ammonia and hydrogen chloride which recombine on cooling — and the same reversible chemistry explains why ammonium salts smell faintly of ammonia when warmed with alkali. The test for ammonium ions follows directly: warm the salt with sodium hydroxide, catch the gas on damp red litmus, and if it turns blue while the smell is pungent the ammonium ion was present. Confirm it with a rod of concentrated hydrochloric acid, which gives white fumes.

items: Catalytic oxidation: 4NH3 + 5O2 → 4NO + 6H2O over platinum at about 800 °C, the start of nitric acid manufacture.
Ammonium chloride on heating dissociates into the two gases, which recombine on cooling as white smoke.
Ammonium ion test: warm with alkali, test the gas with damp red litmus, confirm with hydrochloric acid fumes.
Ammonia also acts as a ligand, forming soluble complex ions with copper and silver salts.

items.text: Testing for ammonium in a salt
items.note: Warm with sodium hydroxide; ammonia is released and turns damp red litmus blue, confirming NH4+.
Ammonia meets hydrogen chloride in air and forms a suspension of tiny solid particles.

items.meaning: Oxygen reaction promoted by a catalyst without the catalyst being consumed.
Breaking apart of a substance into simpler particles, as ammonium chloride does on heating.
Complex ion in which four ammonia molecules coordinate a central metal ion.

learn.title: Uses of ammonia and how they follow from its properties

blocks.text: The economics of ammonia explain most of its uses. Because it holds nitrogen in a form plants can absorb, the great majority is converted into fertilisers: ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate and urea all begin with ammonia. Its high solubility and ease of liquefaction make liquid ammonia an excellent refrigerant in large cold stores, where it evaporates under pressure and absorbs heat. It is the feedstock for nitric acid through catalytic oxidation, and that single chain supplies explosives, dyes and plastics. In the laboratory, dilute aqueous ammonia is one of the two standard reagents for identifying metal ions, and in industry it is used in the Solvay process and in cleaning solutions. Each use traces directly back to one of the properties studied earlier, which is the connection examiners look for.

items: Fertilisers: ammonium salts supply nitrogen to soil in a form roots can take up.
Refrigerant: liquid ammonia vaporises under pressure and absorbs heat, with no chlorine by-products.
Feedstock for nitric acid by catalytic oxidation, which in turn supplies explosives and dyes.
Laboratory reagent for cation identification, and a weak alkali for cleaning and pH adjustment.

items.note: Provides both ammonium and nitrate nitrogen, so plants absorb nitrogen immediately and the soil stores some for later.
Ammonia’s high latent heat of vaporisation removes more heat per kilogram than most alternatives.

keyPoints: Ammonia is prepared by heating ammonium chloride with slaked lime.
It is dried with quicklime and collected in an inverted jar by downward displacement of air because it is lighter than air.
About 700 volumes of ammonia dissolve in one volume of water because of hydrogen bonding.
The fountain experiment shows the pressure drop caused by rapid dissolution.
In water, ammonia accepts a proton to give ammonium and hydroxide ions, making it a weak alkali.
With acids it gives ammonium salts such as ammonium chloride, sulphate and nitrate, used as fertilisers.
With metal salts it precipitates hydroxides: blue copper, dirty green iron(II), reddish brown iron(III), white zinc soluble in excess.
Catalytic oxidation over platinum at 800 °C gives nitric oxide, the first step in nitric acid manufacture.
The test for ammonium ions is warming with alkali and testing the gas with damp red litmus.
Uses: fertilisers, refrigerant, nitric acid feedstock and laboratory reagent.
examFocus: Always give the reason for the drying agent: quicklime because ammonia is alkaline and would react with acidic dryers.
Describe solubility as a pressure effect in the fountain answer rather than quoting a number alone.
The ammonium ion test is three moves: add alkali, warm, test the gas — then confirm with hydrochloric acid fumes.
Connect each use to a property; the examiner awards the link, not the list.

vocabulary.meaning: Calcium hydroxide used with ammonium chloride to prepare ammonia.
Calcium oxide, a basic drying agent suitable for ammonia.
Strong dipole attraction involving hydrogen bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
Oxygen reaction assisted by a catalyst such as platinum.
NH4+, formed when ammonia accepts a proton from water or an acid.
Substance supplying nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium to soil for plant growth.
Base that ionises only partly in water, as aqueous ammonia does.
Bonding of a lone pair from a ligand such as ammonia to a metal ion.

questions.prompt: Ammonia is dried by passing it over:
questions.explanation: Ammonia is alkaline, so only a basic drying agent can be used without reacting with the gas.

questions.prompt: Ammonia is collected in the laboratory by:
options: Upward displacement of air in an upright jar
Downward displacement of air in an inverted jar
questions.answer: Downward displacement of air in an inverted jar
questions.explanation: Ammonia is lighter than air, so the jar is inverted and the heavier air is driven out at the bottom.

questions.prompt: Which ion gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that also dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia?
questions.explanation: Zinc hydroxide is amphoteric and redissolves in excess ammonia to give a colourless complex.

questions.prompt: In the Ostwald process, the oxidation of ammonia requires:
questions.explanation: Platinum-rhodium gauze at high temperature converts ammonia to nitric oxide industrially.

questions.prompt: The pungent gas used in the laboratory preparation is prepared from ammonium chloride and slaked __________.
questions.explanation: Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide; heating it with ammonium chloride drives off ammonia gas.

questions.prompt: In water, ammonia accepts a proton to give ammonium ions and __________ ions, which is why the solution is alkaline.
questions.explanation: The hydroxide ions produced make aqueous ammonia a weak alkali.

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why quicklime is used to dry ammonia instead of concentrated sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Quicklime is a basic drying agent and so does not react with the alkaline ammonia, whereas concentrated sulphuric acid is acidic and would neutralise the gas entirely, absorbing it as ammonium sulphate.
questions.explanation: A drying agent must be chemically inert to the gas being dried, not merely absorbent.

questions.prompt: Describe a test that distinguishes ammonia from hydrogen chloride.
questions.answer: Bring a glass rod dipped in each gas near the other: dense white fumes of ammonium chloride form where they meet. Separately, ammonia turns damp red litmus blue while hydrogen chloride turns damp blue litmus red, and their densities differ, ammonia being the lighter of the two.
questions.explanation: Ammonia is alkaline and hydrogen chloride acidic, so litmus gives opposite results for the two.

questions.prompt: State one use of liquid ammonia and explain the property behind it.
questions.answer: Liquid ammonia is used as a refrigerant in cold storage; it vaporises under pressure and absorbs a large quantity of heat, and it causes no harmful decomposition products.
questions.explanation: Its high heat of vaporisation means a small mass removes a lot of heat.

questions.prompt: Explain, with an equation, why aqueous ammonia behaves as a weak alkali, and describe what happens when it is added to copper(II) sulphate solution.
questions.answer: Ammonia dissolves in water and accepts a proton from a water molecule: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-. The hydroxide ions produced give the alkaline behaviour — turning red litmus blue and neutralising acids — but the equilibrium lies mainly to the left, so only part of the ammonia ionises and it is a weak alkali unlike sodium hydroxide. Added to copper(II) sulphate, the hydroxide ions first precipitate pale blue copper(II) hydroxide; in excess ammonia the precipitate dissolves as ammonia coordinates the copper ion, giving the deep blue tetrammine complex used to confirm copper.
questions.explanation: Proton acceptance creates hydroxide ions, and the incomplete extent of that transfer is precisely what weak means.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation of ammonia, including drying and collection, and give the equation.
questions.answer: Ammonium chloride and slaked lime are mixed and warmed in a flask. The reaction 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3 releases ammonia, which is passed over quicklime to remove the water vapour and then collected in an inverted jar by downward displacement of air, since ammonia is lighter than air. The apparatus is set up promptly and the jar closed as soon as it is full, because ammonia escapes readily and is difficult to keep.
questions.explanation: Reagents, equation, drying choice and collection method together form the complete marking scheme.

questions.prompt: A colourless gas turns damp red litmus blue and gives dense white fumes with hydrogen chloride. A separate salt gives the same gas when warmed with sodium hydroxide. Identify the gas, identify the ion in the salt, and explain why the salt cannot be stored with an acidic drying agent.
questions.answer: The gas is ammonia; its alkalinity turns damp red litmus blue and with hydrogen chloride it forms solid ammonium chloride seen as white fumes. The salt must contain the ammonium ion, since warming with alkali releases ammonia from it. An acidic drying agent cannot be used with that salt because it would neutralise the ammonia as it forms: the acid would convert NH4+ and the released NH3 into a stable ammonium salt such as ammonium sulphate, so no gas would be driven off and the preparation would fail. Only a basic or neutral drying agent is compatible.
questions.explanation: Two signs identify ammonia, and the storage rule follows from the acid-base reactivity that produced the gas in the first place.
